newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Legal showdown in South Korean graft scandal.
newsitem.headline: Legal showdown in South Korean graft scandal.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors moved swiftly on Monday to wrap up the Hanbo graft scandal that has rocked the nation, demanding long jail terms for 11 "immoral" politicians, bankers and businessmen standing trial.
Separately, a former top spy agency official was arrested for bribery.
Kim Ki-sup was sent to a Seoul jail where his close associate Kim Hyun-chul, the son of President Kim Young-sam, was held on Saturday, also accused of taking kickbacks.

Prosecutors demanded a 20-year prison term for Chung Tae-soo, 74, the ailing founder of the Hanbo Group whose steelmaking flagship collapsed in January, sparking a wide-ranging prosecution graft probe.
They also called for a six-year term for Chung's son, Chung Bo-keun, current chairman of the nation's 14th largest business conglomerate.
Father and son are standing trial for bribery and embezzlement along with nine other people in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co under debts of five trillion won ($5.6 billion).
Prosecutors allege that the elder Chung scattered cash among bankers and politicians to keep loans rolling in to fund a massive new steel mill.
The politicians include a former minister and three top aides to Kim Young-sam. In addition to bribery charges, they are accused of influence-peddling.
All defendents appeared in the Seoul District Criminal Court dressed alike in blue prison pyjamas.
"This is a large scale corruption case perpetrated by a collaboration of immoral politicians, bankers and corporate executives," prosecutor Park San-gil told the packed court.
"It has even damaged the nation's reputation."
He said the Hanbo founder, who suffered a stroke after his arrest, "ignored the minimum of corporate and social ethics".
Prosecutors demanded a six-year jail term for former Home Affairs minister Kim Woo-suk.

Kim Ki-sup, the former deputy director of the Agency for National Security Planning, was held on charges of taking 150 million won from the same business executive who allegedly bribed the president's son.
The executive was seeking to win a lucrative cable television licence.
Although judicial proceedings are now speeding to a conclusion, the so-called "Hanbogate" crisis is far from over for president Kim.

Opposition parties say prosecutors have ignored the political sleaze factor beneath the scandal. They claim that loans to Hanbo were a reward for its help in bankrolling the president's 1992 election campaign.
In addition, they claim that the president's son managed leftover funds from the campaign through cronies, including the former intelligence official.
The president, whose image as a graft-fighter has been shattered by the Hanbo loans-for-kickbacks scandal, is expected to make a statement on his campaign financing on Wednesday.

At the court hearing, prosecutors also asked for a 7-1/2 year jail term for ruling New Korea Party lawmaker Hong In-gil, five years each for ruling party lawmakers Hwang Byung-tai and Chung Jae-chull, and seven years for Kwon Roh-kap, an opposition member of parliament.
They requested seven years each for the former president of Korea First Bank, Sheen Kwang-shik, and the onetime head of the Chohung Bank, Woo Chan-mok.
For another former Korea First president, Rhee Chul-soo, they called for an eight-year term.
In addition, prosecutors asked the Seoul District Criminal Court to jail for five years the former financial controller of the Hanbo Group, Kim Jong-kook. ($1=891 won)
